result.title: Preface
result.summary: An RFP for Emerging Markets Equity, issued February 14, 2022 (ID RFP-##-##-##), with email responses due March 31, 2022 at 4:30 p.m. CT; the RFP ID must appear on correspondence. It covers SURS, required services, minimum qualifications, proposal contents, submission procedures, evaluation, timeline, and contacts. Proposal materials include a cover letter, qualifications statement, references, organization and disclosures, and contract information. Submission guidance addresses deadlines, withdrawal, and questions. General conditions cover FOIA disclosure and redacted responses, permitted ordinary-course communications, the SURS quiet period, reserved rights, equal opportunity, and terms. Appendices include minimum qualifications, diversity disclosure, a questionnaire on organization, staffing, investment strategy, risk, clients and services, performance, fees, ESG, trading and internal controls, and other matters; plus a contract addendum, sustainability disclosure, DEI questionnaire, and Morningstar submission.

result.title: I. Introduction
result.summary:
I. Introduction
The State Universities Retirement System (“SURS” or the “System”) is soliciting proposals from qualified firms to provide _________________________ (“Strategies”).
All forms/required documents needed for submitting a Request for Proposal (“RFP”) are available on the SURS website at www.surs.org. A proposer’s preparation and submittal of a proposal or subsequent participation in presentations or contract negotiations creates no obligation on the System to award a contract or to pay any associated costs. All proposals and related materials will be retained by the System and will be subject to disclosure as required in accordance with the Illinois Freedom of Information Act.

result.title: II. Description of SURS
result.summary: SURS is an Illinois public employee retirement system established in 1941 under the Illinois Pension Code. It provides retirement, survivor, disability, and death benefits to over 245,000 members across 61 employers, manages more than $23 billion in diversified investments, and administers a defined-contribution savings plan with about $3.3 billion in assets. Its 11-member board includes five gubernatorial appointees and six elected members and annuitants; trustees serve six-year terms, and the governor appoints the chair. Funding comes from payroll deductions and state employer contributions. SURS employs about 161 staff in Champaign and Naperville, and its latest ACFR is available online. Respondents should know applicable ethics, pension, procurement, and contract requirements, including possible vendor political-contribution restrictions. Illinois law encourages contracting with minority-, women-, and disability-owned businesses and sets a 20% aspirational goal for specified service contracts; such businesses are encouraged to respond. SURS pays the selected provider directly; further vendor requirements appear in Appendix D.

result.title: III. Services Required
result.summary:
III. Services Required
SURS is soliciting proposals from qualified firms to provide _____________________________ Strategies. These strategies, if incorporated into SURS’ portfolio at the conclusion of this search would fall within the _________________________ asset class.

result.title: IV. Minimum Qualifications
result.summary: Proposals are immediately rejected if any minimum qualification is unmet or inadequately documented. Proposers must certify compliance in Appendix A, signed by an authorized representative. Requirements include minimum firm and strategy AUM thresholds (amounts and date left blank; qualified women-, minority-, or disabled-owned firms may be exempt at SURS’ discretion); willingness to accept most-favored-nation pricing; a fee option without performance fees; investment-adviser registration or bank status (or an explanation of exemption), prompt notice of registration changes, Form ADV Parts I and II, and Appendix A certifications; a five-year live emerging-markets equity track record (with the same ownership exemption); an established commingled fund or willingness to create one; required authorizations and available audited financial statements; compliance with applicable legislation and state fiduciary, ethics, and diversity laws; absence of material conflicts with SURS or its board; and compliance with Illinois high-risk home-loan requirements if applicable. Preferred criteria are no material litigation in the past five years (or since inception) and specified public-pension client experience. SURS alone determines qualification and comparability.

result.title: V. Proposal Content
key_items: Statement of Minimum Qualifications; Reference Checks; Company Organization and Disclosures; Contract
result.summary: Proposals must address each requirement separately, include the RFP ID in all communications, and contain an indexed table of contents. An authorized individual must sign the cover letter, which is integral to the proposal; unsigned proposals are rejected. The letter must confirm compliance and offer validity through 30 days after the submission deadline, disclose relevant current relationships or negotiations, and acknowledge possible disclosure under Illinois public-records laws. Proposers must submit the Appendix A Minimum Qualifications Certification; finalists will undergo reference checks. The proposal must include Appendices B, C, E, and F disclosures/questionnaire and firm diversity data submitted through Morningstar’s portal. The RFP is not a contract; SURS may negotiate a contract based on a proposal and alter its terms. Selected candidates must accept Appendix D’s contract terms unless they identify exceptions or questions in their response. SURS need not accept exceptions, which will be discussed during review; changes require mutual agreement in the final contract.

result.title: VI. Submission of Proposals
result.summary:
VI. Submission of Proposals
All proposals must be received no later than the deadline stated in the Anticipated Timeline and Contact Information section. Submissions must be made via email to the identified contact person by the stated deadline. Only email submissions will be accepted.
The proposals become the property of SURS upon submission. All costs for developing proposals and attending presentations and/or interviews are entirely the responsibility of the proposer and shall not be chargeable to SURS.
Only one proposal from an individual, firm, partnership, corporation, or combination thereof, will be considered for this assignment.

result.title: VII. Evaluation Process
key_items: Statement of Minimum Qualifications; Reference Checks; Company Organization and Disclosures; Contract; VI. Submission of Proposals
result.summary: Proposals must include all required information in the prescribed format or be rejected. On-time proposals that pass this pre-review will be assessed by SURS staff and its general consultant, Meketa, for compliance and best fit/value. Evaluation factors, with no stated ranking, include organization, resources, experience, investment team, diversity commitment, performance, fees, fit within SURS’s portfolio, and response detail; fees matter but are not the primary determinant. False or misleading statements, or unsupported references, may result in rejection. The RFP creates no obligation to award a contract or reimburse proposal costs, and does not prevent SURS from obtaining similar services elsewhere. SURS may request additional information or clarification, but proposers may not otherwise change proposals or add information after the deadline. Finalists’ fees may be subject to a discretionary best-and-final offer process.

result.title: X. General Conditions
result.summary: RFP submissions become SURS property and are confidential during selection, but are generally subject to Illinois FOIA afterward. Respondents seeking protection must specifically identify and separate qualifying information, explain competitive harm, and provide a redacted response; pricing is generally disclosable, SURS decides exemptions, and failure to submit redactions may lead to release of the full response. During the publicly announced quiet period, respondents may contact only the designated RFP contact on procurement matters; restrictions apply to discussions, gifts, referrals, and decision-making, subject to limited exceptions, and violations may cause disqualification. SURS may amend the RFP, permit revisions, remove or separately procure services, negotiate terms, request information, and conduct background checks. It need not complete the process or select a vendor, may reject proposals, and will not reimburse proposal costs. SURS commits to equal opportunity and nondiscrimination. Selected respondents may be required to interview or present in Champaign or Chicago without reimbursement and must provide requested documentation before contract award.

nodes.title: Freedom of Information Act Disclosure and Redacted RFP Response Requirement
nodes.summary: All RFP submissions become SURS property and remain confidential during selection, but afterward—including the selected response—are publicly inspectable under Illinois FOIA. Bidders claiming trade secrets or commercial or financial information as proprietary, privileged, or confidential must clearly identify the specific information and explain that disclosure would cause competitive harm (5 ILCS 140/7 and 7.5). Marking every page confidential is insufficient; bidders must make a good-faith effort to designate only qualifying portions.

nodes.title: Redacted Version of RFP Response
key_items: Freedom of Information Act Disclosure and Redacted RFP Response Requirement
nodes.summary: Respondents claiming FOIA exemptions must submit a suitably redacted RFP response; pricing is generally disclosable, and claims for exempt pricing require supporting legal analysis. Failure to provide a redacted version may result in SURS releasing the full response without recourse. SURS determines what is exempt, and material must be identified and separated to be treated as potentially protected. Except for ordinary business, respondents and representatives may contact only the designated RFP contact and must not discuss the RFP with specified SURS personnel or affiliates. The quiet period runs from RFP issuance until vendor selection and successful contract negotiations; its start, continuation, and end are publicly communicated. Restrictions cover communications, gifts, referrals to the Chief Procurement Officer, and decision-making authority, with limited due-diligence and existing-vendor exceptions; violations may disqualify respondents. SURS may amend the RFP and allow proposal revisions, remove services or procure them separately, negotiate added contract terms, request information, and conduct background checks.

nodes.title: SURS RFP Communications and Quiet Period Rules
key_items: Ordinary Course of Business Communications Allowed
nodes.summary: Claims that information is privileged or confidential are not definitive: SURS determines FOIA exemptions, and information must be identified and separated as specified to be considered for protection. Except for normal business matters, RFP respondents and representatives may contact only the listed RFP contact and must not discuss the RFP with SURS-related staff, trustees, advisers, or affiliated parties. The quiet period began when the RFP was issued and ends after Board selection and successful contract negotiations. Its start, continuation, and end must be publicly communicated. Except for search participants and the Chief Procurement Officer or designee, Board members and staff must not discuss related products or services with respondents or accept anything of value from them; contacted Board members must refer respondents to the Chief Procurement Officer. Search authority rests with the Investment Committee, Board, or designees, not individual Board members. Approved due diligence, client conferences, and existing-vendor communications may continue, but procurement and selection discussions are barred. Policy applies throughout the period; violations may disqualify respondents.

nodes.title: Rights Reserved
key_items: Ordinary Course of Business Communications Allowed
nodes.summary: SURS may amend the RFP before selecting a vendor and allow respondents to revise proposals; remove services from consideration or contract for them separately; negotiate additional contract provisions; request more information; and conduct background checks. It is not obligated to complete the process or select a vendor, may reject any or all proposals without prejudice, and will not reimburse proposal-related expenses.

result.title: Appendix A: Statement of Minimum Qualifications
result.summary: Appendix A is a checklist for firms to certify minimum qualifications for an emerging-markets equity proposal, with fields for initials and firm name. Requirements cover minimum firm and strategy assets under management (with thresholds and date left blank); willingness to accept a most-favored-nation pricing clause; a fee proposal offering an option without performance fees; investment-adviser registration or bank status (or an explanation of exemption), prompt notice of status changes, full Form ADV, and required certifications; at least five years of live strategy performance; an existing or commitment-dependent commingled fund; required legal authorizations and availability of audited financial statements; compliance with applicable legislation and state fiduciary, ethics, diversity, and disclosure rules; absence of material conflicts with SURS or its board; and compliance with applicable High-Risk Home Loan Act requirements for Illinois finance entities. Qualified women-, minority-, or disabled-owned firms are exempt from the asset and track-record requirements and may receive further consideration at SURS’ discretion. Signature, date, and title fields are provided. Appendix B is a separate SURS diversity disclosure attachment.

result.title: Appendix B: SURS Diversity Disclosure (Separate Attachment)
key_items: Service Provider Reporting; Note: Please provide numeric responses
result.summary: Appendix B is a SURS diversity disclosure form requesting firm/contact details and employee data for U.S. citizens or permanent residents, categorized by staff role, gender, race/ethnicity, and disability. Respondents provide numeric counts and percentages; each person selects one race/ethnicity category, with disability recorded additionally. The form also collects contract counts and expenses for MWDBE service providers and for non-MWDBE providers where more than half the work is performed by racial/ethnic minorities, women, or persons with disabilities, for a stated 12-month period. Additional diversity-program information may be attached, and an authorized official signs and dates the disclosure. SURS explains the data supports Illinois Pension Code reporting and diversity goals. Appendix C instructs RFP respondents to answer questions in order and includes contact/company information fields and Part 1 organization questions on organization and product names, address, product inception, firm/product AUM, and benchmark.

result.title: Appendix C: Questionnaire
result.summary: Appendix C provides a sample RFP questionnaire to be answered in order, with contact and company details. It covers organizational background, ownership, services, institutional experience, diversity, registration, litigation, insurance, financial condition, audits, and GIPS; staffing, personnel qualifications and continuity, diversity, compensation, retention, and regulatory/legal history; and the proposed strategy’s philosophy, research, portfolio construction, return sources, tools, and changes. Risk questions address guidelines, limits, monitoring, liquidity, tracking error, compliance, conflicts, and controls. Client and service questions cover capacity, liquidity, assets, accounts, major clients, flows, and losses. Performance questions request return records, GIPS disclosures, attribution, and portfolio characteristics. Fee schedules, vehicle terms, expenses, and negotiability are requested, as are ESG commitments, integration, monitoring, engagement, and proxy voting. Trading and internal-control topics include systems, brokers, costs, violations, diverse-vendor trading, personal trading, and reconciliation. Other requests cover ADV, continuity planning, legal and regulatory matters, ethics, conflicts, reporting, meetings, marketing materials, additional disclosures, and placement-agent use and compensation.

nodes.title: PART 1: ORGANIZATION
key_items: Appendix C: Q u e s t i o n n a i r e
nodes.summary: An organization due-diligence questionnaire requests firm and product names, addresses, launch date, assets under management, benchmark and proposed vehicle; contracting entity; a brief overview of offerings and services; experience managing the relevant strategies for public pensions and other institutions, business share, and historical changes; firm history, ownership and structure, and any non-asset-management businesses. It seeks firm and mandate-team staffing, diversity, founding/SEC-registration dates, locations, parent, ownership percentages, and details of subsidiary or outside-owner relationships and influence. It asks about MWDBE certification and an organizational chart; registration, litigation, regulatory judgments, insurance, bonding, GIPS compliance and auditor; and explanations of litigation or judgments. Supporting materials include an insurance certificate, financial-condition information, insurance coverage amounts and carriers, and audit timing, auditor, findings, and auditor changes.

nodes.title: PART 2: STAFFING
nodes.summary: Part 2 requests staffing and regulatory information for the investment product: an RFP contact’s name, title, address, phone, and email; personnel counts by role, product dedication/involvement, and demographic categories; the firm’s employee and ownership diversity efforts, policies, evolution, and competitive benefits; and team structure, staffing, and portfolio-manager client duties. It requests key personnel details, including education, titles, experience, tenure, and product involvement; other duties, analyst contributions to other strategies, backup arrangements, client-service availability, five-year personnel arrivals/departures, biographies, decision-maker continuity, and succession planning. Firms must report product-related staff gains and losses over three years with reasons, describe compensation and incentive allocation, and explain talent retention. Finally, it asks about required regulatory registrations; agency audits or actions in the prior seven years and resulting changes; product-associated employees’ investigations, litigation, or regulatory actions in the prior five years; and relevant legal judgments or pending cases involving current or former employees.

nodes.title: PART 3: INVESTMENT STRATEGY
nodes.summary: Part 3 is a questionnaire about a proposed investment strategy. It asks for submitted strategy names and eVestment listings; an elevator pitch; product differentiators, philosophy, objectives, approach, benchmark, and portfolio role; top-down/bottom-up methods and style; research informing development and expected alpha persistence; return, risk, and valuation models; regional, country, sector, and security allocation; and portfolio construction stages, quantitative and qualitative research, information and idea sources, model-portfolio use, account deviations, and sell discipline. It also covers currency hedging, current or historical portfolio issues, expected returns and the percentage contribution and sustainability of added-value sources (sector and security selection, factor/style tilts, trading, and other sources), software and quantitative tools, systematic or discretionary processes and repeatability, monitored risks and guideline controls, and performance-impacting events and investment-process or model changes since inception.

nodes.title: PART 4: RISK CONTROL
nodes.summary: The section requests internal investment guidelines and a policy-limits table covering cash, market capitalization, position size, sector, industry, country, and currency hedging, including whether limits apply and their absolute or benchmark-relative maximums or ranges. It asks how the firm defines risk and its philosophy; its risk-control process, portfolio-construction models and controls, use of cash, and monitoring of factor exposures; how investment style and process adherence are monitored and by whom; and how liquidity risk and illiquidity events are handled. It also asks for expected absolute and relative returns and volatility, the role and management of benchmark tracking error, and systems for monitoring client guidelines. Finally, it asks whether the firm has an in-house Compliance Department, how internal controls prevent conflicts in employee, proprietary, and discretionary client trading, and how compliance and regulatory policies and procedures are communicated.

nodes.title: PART 5: CLIENT BASE AND SERVICES
nodes.summary: Requests information on product capacity and its calculation; expected soft and hard closes, including amounts and timing; and estimated liquidation times for 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of the strategy. It seeks year-end firm and product assets and account counts, including institutional, tax-exempt/taxable, and client-type breakdowns consistent with eVestment data. It requests the ten largest product clients’ type, retention date, AUM, and tax-exempt status; and contact details and market values for the three largest U.S. public pension clients, with permission sought before contact. Finally, it asks for three years of firmwide and product account and asset gains/losses, including public-fund figures and reasons for losses or material changes, plus historical firmwide, public-fund, and product assets and client counts.

nodes.title: PART 6: PERFORMANCE / QUANTITATIVE CHARACTERISTICS
nodes.summary: Part 6 requests performance and quantitative information: monthly net- and gross-of-fee returns since inception through December 31, submitted to eVestment Alliance and in Excel, in chronological order without aggregation gaps and labeled by product name, vehicle type, and fee basis. It asks for the applicable GIPS compliance level and composite disclosures; an explanation of performance evaluation, attribution methods and tools, and how attribution informs management; and strategy attribution for the latest three- and five-year periods ending December 31. It also requests portfolio characteristics for the past three calendar years, or since inception if shorter, including holdings, turnover, market-cap measures, yield, valuation, growth, ROE, active share, tracking error, and cash; portfolio weights across market-cap bands; sector and regional allocations; and the weighted top ten holdings.

nodes.title: PART 7: FEES
nodes.summary: Part 7 covers fees. It asks for the standard fee schedule for all vehicles offered, with vehicle options including institutional commingled fund, institutional mutual fund, separate account, or other. Requested details include product name, vehicle entity type, minimum initial and subsequent investments, minimum asset level, subscription and redemption frequency, redemption notice and cash-proceeds periods, minimum fee, sample fee schedule and calculation, estimated annual operating expenses, operating-expense cap, and any redemption penalties. It also requests a proposed schedule if different from the standard schedule, including all-in fees and the management-fee versus operating-expense breakdown specified in Appendix F; this schedule will be used for evaluation. Finally, it asks whether the proposed fees are negotiable.

nodes.title: PART 8: ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND GOVERNANCE (ESG) CONSIDERATIONS
nodes.summary: The section asks about the firm’s ESG commitments and practices: PRI or similar signatory status and its latest assessment; sustainability reporting, frequency, availability, and ESG’s role in investment decisions; whether it has an ESG policy; and how ESG is integrated into strategy, security analysis, and portfolio construction. It asks which ESG factors are assessed, data sources, and how materiality is weighed; how ESG issues are systematically monitored and by whom; whether staff or other resources are dedicated to ESG; how the firm engages company management on material concerns and evaluates engagement; and whether its proxy-voting policy incorporates ESG, including its implementation process.

nodes.title: PART 9: TRADING PRACTICES/INTERNAL CONTROL
nodes.summary: The section asks about the firm’s compliance system and implementation; internal controls, compliance officer, periodic risk assessments, and internal audit; trading staff, desk coverage, headcount, locations, and tenure; trading systems, methods, venues, and brokers; any client-guideline violations and their resolution; electronic trade monitoring and how trading costs are monitored and reduced. It also asks about the firm’s ability to execute and track brokerage through minority-, women-, and disability-owned firms (MWDBE), including firm-wide and strategy-specific equity-trade percentages, and its approach to working with diverse vendors, partners, and clients. Finally, it requests the personal trading policy and procedures, and details on client-transaction reconciliation, including reconciliation frequency for client and custodian position records and review of client cash positions.

nodes.title: PART 10: OTHER
nodes.summary: Requests the firm’s SEC Form ADV; an overview of business continuity and disaster recovery, including server locations and management, offsite workstations, and VPN access; details of in-house or external legal support; regulatory visits, outcomes, and anticipated examinations; and independent litigators or accountants and their services. It asks about the Code of Ethics, employee compliance and enforcement, potential mandate conflicts, client reporting and a sample package, underlying-holdings transparency and SURS online access, portfolio review calls, investor meetings, and annual strategic outlooks. It also requests a recent pitch book and factsheet, and invites disclosure of other relevant information. Finally, it asks whether external placement agents are used or compensated, the assets and mandates involved and compensation arrangements, whether unregistered third parties solicited government business, and whether an agent was used for this specific search and its identity and compensation.

result.title: Appendix D: Addendum to Contract
result.summary: The addendum requires the contractor to certify, where applicable, that an individual is not in educational-loan default; it is not barred for bribery or bid-rigging/rotation and complies with procurement laws; it will maintain a drug-free workplace; and it does not participate in prohibited international boycotts. Fees or commissions connected to the contract must be disclosed, with SURS notified if that certification changes. Contractors subject to Illinois law must prevent employment discrimination, take affirmative action, follow human-rights procedures, provide requested information, and maintain sexual-harassment policies covering illegality, definitions, examples, complaints and penalties, remedies, agency contacts, and anti-retaliation. Applicable prevailing-wage requirements must be followed. Records supporting contract disbursements must be retained for five years after completion and made available for audits. Contractors must notify SURS’s Ethics Officer of employment solicitations to SURS employees and acknowledge applicable open-meetings and freedom-of-information laws. The agreement may be executed in counterparts, including electronically. The contractor also certifies its federal tax ID under penalty of perjury and identifies its business entity type.

result.title: Appendix E: Sustainability Disclosure (Separate Attachment)
result.summary: Appendix E provides a sample SURS sustainability disclosure required under 30 ILCS 238/10 for potential investment managers. The form requests firm, strategy, address, and contact details, plus an explanation of how sustainability factors are integrated into investment decisions, analysis, portfolio construction, due diligence, and ownership to support risk-adjusted returns, identify risks, and meet fiduciary duties. An authorized official certifies the information by signing and providing their name, title, and date. It also lists the Illinois Sustainable Investing Act’s five sustainability-factor categories: corporate governance and leadership; environmental impacts; social capital and relationships with external stakeholders; human capital and workforce practices; and business model and innovation, including resilience, supply chains, product life cycles, and climate-related physical impacts. Examples include board independence, emissions, human rights, worker safety, diversity, and resource efficiency.

result.title: Appendix F: DEI Questionnaire
result.summary: The SURS DEI Questionnaire requests information and supporting documents on firm policies and programs: DEI policies and committees; equal pay; mentorship, sponsorship and affinity programs; diversity goals, outcomes and compensation; anonymous reporting and investigation of harassment, discrimination and violence; MWDB hiring improvements and certifications; DEI review of service providers, provider codes of conduct, and use of MWDBE investment banks. It also asks about employee conduct codes, mandatory anti-harassment and nondiscrimination training, and related claims involving current or former employees over the past five years and the firm’s responses. Initiatives covered include partnerships and programs supporting the attraction and retention of women, minorities and people with disabilities in investment, and actions against racism and sexism in the industry during the past year. Firms are asked to complete the attached SURS Diversity Disclosure. Terms for covered individuals and businesses follow definitions in the Illinois Business Enterprise for Minorities, Women, and Persons with Disabilities Act.

result.title: Appendix G: Morningstar Submission (Separate Attachment)
result.summary: Appendix G directs firms to submit firm-level diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) data through Morningstar’s free Institutional Data Manager (IDM) at idm.morningstar.com; more information is in the Morningstar Diversity Data Toolkit. Rising investor demand and regulatory changes make transparent workforce and ownership data important for investment decisions, accountability, and stronger business ecosystems. IDM provides a standardized, centralized reporting process with review and editing, quality checks, and direct availability in Morningstar Direct, reducing reporting and collection burdens while supporting analytics, screening, assurance tools, performance analysis, supply-chain assessment, compliance, and marketing. Data examples include ownership by gender, disability, race and ethnicity; board and employee demographics by role and identity; DEI policies, conduct procedures, hiring and workplace practices, talent, investment criteria, and certifications; portfolio-manager demographics; and diverse-provider utilization, contracts, and expenses. Submission is complimentary, and firms may report additional firm or strategy data or contact their Success Representative or idm@morningstar.com. The document also includes a 2021 copyright and restrictions on unauthorized reproduction.
